title: The Floating Torii and the Mountain of Fire
subtitle: Pass the Tide-Gate of the Sea-Dragon, Climb the Mountain of Fire, and Break the Crown of the Oni-King 🌋⛩️

setting.name: Itsukushima and Fuji-no-yama, the Floating World
setting.description: The Floating World (Ukiyo) is a mythic mirror of feudal Japan, where the boundary between the seen world and the spirit world thins at dawn and dusk. The campaign's finale spans two sacred places. The first is Itsukushima, a holy island in the Inland Sea so revered that no birth or death is permitted upon its soil — and from its shallows rises a colossal vermilion torii gate that, at high tide, appears to float upon the water like a dream made of cinnabar and cedar. The second is Fuji-no-yama, the Mountain of Fire: a perfect snow-capped cone that the people regard as a goddess and a god both, climbed by pilgrims through ten numbered stations to its smoking summit crater. Beneath the mountain's serene white slopes, the Oni-King Akki-no-Kami has gathered a host of demons, intending to crack the crater open and drown the Floating World in fire and ash.
setting.atmosphere: Sacred stillness shot through with rising dread. On Itsukushima, the air smells of salt, incense, and grilled rice; tame deer wander the lantern-lit paths and the great torii glows like a coal as the tide swallows the flats. On Fuji, the world thins — pilgrims' bells fade, the cedar gives way to scoured volcanic gravel, the air goes cold and sharp and hard to breathe, and a sulfur reek drifts down from the summit where the sky itself seems to hold its breath. Beauty and danger braid together at every elevation; the closer the party draws to the crater, the more the mountain's calm mask slips to reveal the furnace beneath.

keyLocations.name: Itsukushima — The Floating Torii and the Sea-Shrine
keyLocations.description: A shrine of vermilion pillars and cedar walkways built out over the tidal flats so that, at high tide, the entire complex and its great offshore torii gate seem to float upon the sea. The torii stands roughly a hundred paces out from the shrine, its twin pillars sunk into the seabed, its crossbeams painted the deep red of cinnabar. At low tide the seabed is exposed and pilgrims walk out across rippled wet sand to press coins into the gate's barnacled base; at high tide the water rises chest-deep and only a boat will carry you there. The shrine is tended by miko (shrine maidens) and a single ancient guardian who is more than she appears.
features: The great vermilion torii standing offshore, walkable at low tide and surrounded by chest-deep water at high tide
A cedar-plank shrine raised on pillars above the tidal flat, connected by covered walkways that hum faintly at dawn
A tide that turns roughly every six hours — a posted tide-board (and the miko) tell pilgrims when the flats will flood
Stone lanterns lining the approach, lit each dusk, their reflections doubling across the wet sand
encounters: A trial of worthiness set by the sea-dragon Ryūjin-no-Musume, the shrine's hidden guardian, who tests the party before granting passage to Fuji
Drowned-dead (umibōzu spawn) that rise from the flats at the turn of the tide if the party trespasses to the gate unblessed
A race against the incoming tide to retrieve an offering left at the torii's base before the flats flood
secrets: The ancient miko who greets the party is Ryūjin-no-Musume herself, daughter of the sea-dragon-god, wearing a mortal shape to judge pilgrims
The torii is a tide-gate: at the precise slack of high tide, with the proper offering, it opens a brief passage of calm water that ferries the worthy toward the foot of Fuji in a single night

keyLocations.name: Hakone — The Hot Springs at the Mountain's Foot
keyLocations.description: A green valley of steaming pools and lacquered bathhouses cupped between forested ridges, the last comfort before the climb. Sulphur-scented steam drifts from the rocks, mineral water gathers in stone basins hot enough to redden the skin, and a torii-marked path leads up out of the cedars toward Fuji's lower slopes. Pilgrims rest here, soak their travel-worn limbs, buy walking-staves and straw sandals, and pray at the trailhead shrine before beginning the ascent.
features: Open-air onsen (hot spring baths) whose mineral waters grant a measure of healing and restful sleep before the climb
A trailhead shrine where pilgrims have a staff branded with the first station's mark for a few coins
A teahouse selling provisions: dried rations, oilcloth, charcoal hand-warmers, and the local maple-leaf cakes
An old mountain guide, Jirō, who knows Fuji's moods and warns which season the mountain permits climbing
encounters: Roleplay with Jirō the guide and other pilgrims, gathering warnings about the Oni-King's demons on the upper slopes
A band of oni scouts (ogres) descended to the springs to defile the sacred water and waylay pilgrims
A long soak in the onsen that restores the party before the ascent (functions as a short rest with benefits)
secrets: Jirō climbed Fuji as a young man and saw the crater's demon-gate; he has never spoken of it until now and bears a charm that wards a single mind against fear
One bathhouse pool is fed by a spring that runs straight from Fuji's heart — its water glows faintly when the mountain stirs, a living barometer of the Oni-King's progress

keyLocations.name: Fuji's Lower Slopes — The Cedar Stations (First through Fifth)
keyLocations.description: The pilgrim trail switchbacks up through ancient cedar forest, past numbered stations — small huts and shrines where climbers rest, refill water, and have their staves branded. The lower stations are green and gentle; by the Fifth Station the great trees thin to gnarled, wind-bent scrub and the first bare volcanic gravel appears underfoot. This is the threshold where the ordinary world is left behind and the climb proper begins. The Oni-King's lesser demons have begun raiding the stations, scattering pilgrims and snuffing the shrine-fires.
features: Numbered station huts (First through Fifth) offering rest, water, and staff-branding
A pilgrim trail of switchbacks rising through cedar forest to the treeline at the Fifth Station
Wooden trail-shrines marking the boundary between the mundane and sacred slopes
The first thin, cold air at the Fifth Station — a noticeable shortness of breath for the unacclimatized
encounters: Tengu raiders (use harpy/swarm tactics, reflavored as crow-winged mountain goblins) ambushing pilgrims along the switchbacks
A burning station hut whose keeper and pilgrims must be saved before the flames spread
A landslide hazard where demon-loosened scree threatens to sweep the party off the trail
secrets: A station keeper hides a kakemono (scroll painting) of Fuji that, when held to the summit, reveals the demon-gate's true location at the crater's eastern lip
The trail-shrines, prayed at in order, grant a cumulative blessing that resists the demon-cold higher up

keyLocations.name: Fuji's Upper Slopes — The Ash Stations (Sixth through Ninth)
keyLocations.description: Above the treeline, Fuji becomes a different world: a steep, endless slope of red-black volcanic cinder and gravel, raked by freezing wind, the air so thin that each step is labored and the head pounds. The numbered stations here are stone-walled huts braced against the gales, their lamps the only warmth for miles. By night, climbers traditionally push for the summit in darkness to catch the dawn. But the Oni-King's host now holds the upper stations, and the demon-cold bites deeper than any natural frost. Goraikō — the holy sunrise — is said to be visible from the summit, if one can reach it before the mountain's master does.
features: Stone mountain-huts (Sixth through Ninth Station) where climbers shelter from wind and cold, now contested by demons
A near-vertical cinder slope where loose gravel makes every step a struggle (difficult terrain, exhaustion-inducing)
Thin air and brutal cold imposing altitude and exposure hazards (see Act 3 mechanics)
A pre-dawn push tradition: the safest window to crest the summit is in the cold dark before goraikō, the sunrise
encounters: Oni shock-troops (ogres and an ogre champion) holding the Eighth Station as a forward camp
A yuki-onna (snow-woman; use a reflavored will-o'-wisp + cold elemental) luring stragglers off the trail to freeze
Altitude-sickness and frostbite saving throws that escalate with each station climbed
secrets: The Ninth Station's hut conceals a forgotten warrior-monk's grave whose buried naginata is a +1 weapon blessed against oni
A hidden ice-cave behind the Eighth Station offers a sheltered long rest out of the demon-wind, if found

keyLocations.name: The Summit Crater — The Demon-Gate of Akki-no-Kami
keyLocations.description: The roof of the Floating World: a vast circular crater of cracked black stone wreathed in sulfurous steam, the rim ringed with the broken shrines of pilgrims past. At the crater's eastern lip the rising sun should bless the goraikō — but the Oni-King Akki-no-Kami has torn open a demon-gate here, a fissure of molten light through which his lieutenants pour, and he means to shatter the crater's seal and wake the fire-mountain to ruin the world below. To stand on this rim is to stand between heaven's light and the earth's furnace. Here the campaign's climactic battle is fought.
features: A vast steaming crater of cracked obsidian, rimmed with the toppled shrines and offerings of centuries of pilgrims
The demon-gate: a molten fissure at the eastern lip pouring heat and lesser demons into the world
The eastern rim where goraikō, the holy sunrise, breaks — a place of true power if the seal can be restored at dawn
Treacherous footing of loose scree and superheated stone around the gate (hazard: 1d6 fire damage to anyone shoved or knocked into the steam vents)
encounters: The climactic battle against the Oni-King Akki-no-Kami and his demon honor-guard
Waves of lesser oni and fire-imps pouring from the demon-gate until the gate is sealed
The dawn-sealing: restoring the crater's seal as goraikō breaks, which can turn the tide if the party survives long enough
secrets: Akki-no-Kami's iron crown is the source of his power over the gate; striking it from his brow (a called shot or a critical) weakens his hold and slows the demon tide
If Ryūjin-no-Musume's tide-blessing was earned on Itsukushima, the rising sun at goraikō can be channeled through the offering to slam the demon-gate shut — but only at the precise moment of dawn

synopsis: At the climax of their journey through the Floating World, the heroes are summoned to the holy island of Itsukushima, where the great vermilion torii floats upon the high tide and a sea-dragon's daughter guards the way. There they must prove themselves worthy and earn the tide-gate's blessing, for word has come that the Oni-King Akki-no-Kami has seized the sacred Mountain of Fire, Fuji-no-yama, and means to tear open its crater to drown the world in ash. Ferried across the inland sea by the dragon's grace, the party rests at the hot springs of Hakone before beginning the great ascent — climbing through the numbered stations and mountain huts, battling tengu raiders and oni shock-troops, enduring the killing cold and thin air of the upper slopes, until at last they crest the summit crater at the edge of the holy sunrise to break the Oni-King's crown, seal the demon-gate, and decide the fate of the Floating World.
hook: A storm-petrel falls exhausted at the party's feet bearing a strip of prayer-paper inked by the miko of Itsukushima: the mountain-god of Fuji has gone silent, the sacred fires of the summit shrines have all gone out, and pilgrims who climbed have not returned. The shrine maidens beg the heroes to come to the floating torii at the next high tide, for only there can the sea-dragon's daughter grant the blessing needed to face what now crowns the Mountain of Fire. The petrel dies with the dawn — and far to the north-east, a thread of black smoke rises from Fuji's perfect white cone for the first time in living memory. 🌊⛩️

acts.title: Act 1: The Tide-Gate of the Floating Torii ⛩️🌊
acts.description: The party arrives at the holy island of Itsukushima, navigates the rhythm of its tides, and earns the trial and blessing of Ryūjin-no-Musume, the sea-dragon's daughter, at the floating torii. This act emphasizes wonder, ritual, social play, and a single sharp combat against the drowned-dead, establishing the stakes and granting the tide-blessing the party will need at the very end.
objectives: Arrive at Itsukushima and learn the rhythm of the tides from the miko
Make a proper offering at the floating torii, timing the walk against the incoming tide
Pass the trial set by the disguised guardian Ryūjin-no-Musume
Earn the tide-blessing and passage toward Fuji

scenes.name: The Island Where None May Die
scenes.description: The party's boat approaches Itsukushima at evening, the great torii burning vermilion against the darkening sea. Tame deer wander the lantern-lit shore, and the miko receive the heroes with grave courtesy, explaining the island's sanctity and the silence that has fallen over Fuji to the north-east.
scenes.readAloud: "Your boat glides across water gone copper with sunset, and there — rising straight out of the sea — stands the great gate. Two vast pillars of vermilion cedar, crowned with sweeping crossbeams the deep red of cinnabar, the whole thing seeming to float upon the tide with no land beneath it at all. Beyond it, the shrine itself stands on stilts above the water, its covered walkways glowing with the light of a hundred stone lanterns. Tame deer pick their way along the shoreline and turn liquid black eyes toward you without fear. A young shrine maiden in white and crimson waits at the jetty, her hands folded. 'Welcome, travelers, to the island where none may be born and none may die,' she says softly. 'You have come about the mountain. Good. The sea has been waiting for you.'"

skillChecks.success: You recall that Itsukushima is so sacred that births and deaths are forbidden on its soil, and that its torii is said to be a gate between the sea-realm and the land of the living.
skillChecks.failure: You sense the island is holy but cannot place its particular customs.

skillChecks.success: The young miko who greets you carries herself with a stillness far older than her years — and when a wave breaks against the jetty, for just a heartbeat her shadow on the planks is not shaped like a girl, but like something vast and serpentine.
skillChecks.failure: She seems an ordinary, if unusually composed, shrine maiden.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Establish reverence and wonder. The deer are tame and may nose at the party's packs looking for food (a chance for charm and levity). The lead miko is secretly Ryūjin-no-Musume; drop subtle hints (her shadow, her knowledge, the deference the other miko show her) but do not reveal it yet. She explains the tides turn roughly every six hours and that to honor the gate, one must walk out to it at low tide and return before the flood — a test of timing and respect.

scenes.name: The Offering and the Turning Tide
scenes.description: The party walks out across the exposed tidal flats to the base of the floating torii to leave an offering, but the tide turns sooner than expected — and the drowned-dead rise from the flooding sand to drag down those who would defile the gate without a true heart. The party must complete the offering and win back to the shrine before the flats fully flood.
scenes.readAloud: "At low tide the sea draws back to reveal a vast plain of rippled wet sand, and you walk out toward the great gate that had seemed to float and now stands revealed on bare ground, its barnacled pillars thicker than ancient oaks. Pilgrims before you have pressed coins into the cracks of its base for luck. But as you reach it, you feel the change underfoot — the sand darkening, water threading up between your toes, the distant line of the sea folding back toward you faster than any tide should. From the wet sand around the pillars, pale shapes begin to rise: drowned things with sea-glass eyes and mouths full of silt, reaching for your ankles. The tide is coming in, and it is bringing the dead with it."

skillChecks.success: You read the tide-board and the wet sand correctly and know you have roughly three rounds before the flats flood to chest depth — plan your retreat accordingly.
skillChecks.failure: You misjudge the tide; it floods a round sooner than expected, costing the party precious time.

skillChecks.success: You press your offering into the gate with the proper words and a bow; the nearest drowned-dead recoil from the gesture, buying the party a round and granting advantage against them.
skillChecks.failure: Your offering is hurried and graceless; the dead are not appeased and press the attack.

skillChecks.success: You wade and slog back through the rising water to the shrine walkway before the flats fully flood.
skillChecks.failure: The chest-deep flood catches you; you are swept 20 feet and must make a DC 13 Strength save to avoid being pulled under for 1d4 cold damage.

enemies: 4 drowned-dead (use ghoul stats, reflavored as umibōzu spawn)
1 will-o'-wisp (a drowned lantern-light luring the unwary deeper onto the flats)
combatEncounters.tactics: The drowned-dead claw up from the sand to grapple and drag characters toward the deepening water, where the flood will finish them. The lantern-light hovers farther out, trying to lure pursuers off the safe sandbar into chest-deep water. The whole fight is a race: every round the water rises, turning more of the flats into difficult terrain and eventually chest-deep hazard. The dead crumble to silt at the true turn of high tide if the party has made a proper offering.
combatEncounters.terrain: Open tidal flats flooding in real time. Round 1: damp sand (normal). Round 2: ankle-deep (difficult terrain in a 30-ft band). Round 3+: chest-deep flood spreading outward (swimming, disadvantage on melee, current pulls 10 ft toward the sea each round). The torii base offers the only high ground.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is a tense set-piece combining combat with the environmental clock of the tide. Reward players who track the tide and retreat in good order. The drowned-dead are not the true threat — the rising sea is. If the party panics and lingers, let the flood do real work. A proper, respectful offering (the Religion check) is the key that dispels the dead at high tide's slack; brute force alone is slower and more dangerous.
loot: Sea-pearls pressed into the torii's base by old pilgrims, freed by the fighting (worth 40 gp total)
A waterlogged offering-box on the sandbar containing 25 gp and a vial of holy water
A drowned pilgrim's brass tide-compass that always points to the nearest safe shore (minor wondrous item)

scenes.name: The Trial of the Sea-Dragon's Daughter
scenes.description: At the slack of high tide, with the offering made and the dead laid to rest, the young miko reveals her true nature as Ryūjin-no-Musume, daughter of the sea-dragon-god. She sets the party a trial of worthiness — a test of honesty, courage, or compassion rather than strength — and, if they pass, grants them the tide-blessing they will need at the summit of Fuji.
scenes.readAloud: "The flood reaches its height and goes utterly still — slack tide, the sea holding its breath. The great torii floats again upon glassy water, lit from within by the rising moon. The young miko walks out across the surface of the sea toward you, her feet leaving rings upon the water, and as she comes her form unfolds: scales of pearl and storm-grey, eyes like deep green tide-pools, a body that coils vast and serpentine beneath the gentle face. 'I am Ryūjin-no-Musume, daughter of the dragon who holds the sea,' she says, and her voice is the sound of waves on stone. 'The mountain-god has fallen silent because a king of demons sits upon his crown. You would climb to break that crown. So. Let me see whether you are worth the blessing I would spend on you.'"

skillChecks.success: You answer the dragon's questions with honesty and humility, naming both your strengths and your failings; she judges you worthy and grants the tide-blessing freely.
skillChecks.failure: You boast or evade; the dragon is unimpressed and sets a harder test, withholding part of the blessing's power.

skillChecks.success: You perceive that the dragon does not want flattery or feats of arms — she wants proof the party climbs to protect others, not for glory. Answer accordingly and she warms to you.
skillChecks.failure: You misread her and offer the wrong kind of proof, lengthening the trial.

skillChecks.success: If a character honors her with a song, dance, story, or prayer worthy of the sea, the dragon is moved and offers a boon beyond the blessing.
skillChecks.failure: A clumsy offering is politely received but earns no extra favor.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is a roleplay-driven trial; there is no combat unless the party is foolish enough to attack a dragon-god (do not script this as winnable). The trial should be tailored to the party — a test of honesty, of compassion, of courage, or of self-knowledge. Passing grants the TIDE-BLESSING: a token (a vial of slack-tide water, or a pearl) that, at the precise moment of goraikō (dawn) on Fuji's summit, can channel the rising sun to slam the demon-gate shut. Make clear (through the dragon's own words) that this blessing is the linchpin of the finale. She also offers passage: her tide will carry the party's boat to the foot of Fuji in a single night.
loot: The Tide-Blessing — a vial of slack-tide seawater (or a storm-grey pearl) that can seal the demon-gate at dawn (key plot item for Act 4)
Ryūjin's scale, worn as a charm, granting the bearer the ability to breathe water for 1 hour, once
If the Performance boon is earned: a Potion of Water Breathing for the whole party, and the dragon's promise of one rescue at sea

acts.title: Act 2: The Springs of Hakone and the First Stations 🌸♨️
acts.description: Ferried by the dragon's tide to the mainland, the party rests at the hot springs of Hakone, gathers warnings and provisions, then begins the ascent of Fuji through the cedar stations. This act blends restful roleplay with the first real demon-combats as the Oni-King's raiders contest the lower slopes.
objectives: Rest and resupply at the Hakone hot springs
Learn the mountain's dangers from Jirō the guide
Drive off the oni scouts defiling the sacred spring
Climb the cedar stations (First through Fifth) and reach the treeline

scenes.name: The Steaming Valley
scenes.description: The dragon's tide deposits the party at dawn on the green shore below Hakone. Steam rises from the forested valley, and the heroes find the last comfort before the climb: hot spring baths, a trailhead shrine, a teahouse of warm cakes, and an old guide who has seen what waits above.
scenes.readAloud: "You wake on a pebbled shore as the dragon's tide withdraws, and the land rises before you in green ridges veiled with drifting steam. Hakone: a valley of hot springs, where sulphur-scented mist curls from the rocks and stone basins brim with mineral water hot enough to redden the skin. Lacquered bathhouses cling to the slopes, a torii-marked path leads up toward the cedars, and beyond it all — impossibly vast, impossibly white — Fuji-no-yama fills the northern sky, a perfect cone of snow with, you now see, a single thin thread of black smoke rising from its summit. An old man tending a teahouse looks up, follows your gaze to that smoke, and his face goes grave. 'So,' he says. 'It is as bad as the petrels said.'"

skillChecks.success: You recognize the onsen's mineral waters as genuinely restorative; a long soak will mend aches and ready the body for the cold thin air above (treat as a short rest that also removes one level of exhaustion).
skillChecks.failure: You enjoy the bath but gain no special benefit.

skillChecks.success: You win old Jirō's trust; he shares hard-won knowledge of Fuji's stations, the killing cold above the treeline, and the demon-gate he glimpsed at the crater as a young man.
skillChecks.failure: Jirō is wary of outsiders and shares only general warnings about the climb.

scenes.roleplayNotes: A breather scene of warmth and humanity before the climb. Let the players soak, buy provisions (rations, oilcloth, charcoal hand-warmers, walking staves, the local maple-leaf cakes), and roleplay with pilgrims and with Jirō. Jirō is the lorekeeper for the ascent: he explains the numbered stations, the tradition of the pre-dawn summit push to catch goraikō, the very real danger of the thin air, and — reluctantly — the demon-gate. He offers his fear-warding charm to whoever seems steadiest. Foreshadow the altitude mechanics here so they don't feel arbitrary later.
loot: Provisions for the climb: 10 days' rations, oilcloth, 4 charcoal hand-warmers (each negates cold-exposure disadvantage for 1 hour)
Jirō's fear-ward charm: the bearer has advantage on saves against being frightened (one charm, give to the party)
A bundle of momiji-manjū (maple-leaf cakes, 6) — eating one restores 1 hit point and a little morale

scenes.name: Demons at the Sacred Spring
scenes.description: As the party prepares to begin the ascent, a band of oni scouts descends to the springs to foul the sacred water and waylay pilgrims. The heroes must drive them off before the demons poison the onsen and the trailhead shrine.
scenes.readAloud: "Steam hisses and a stench of carrion rolls down the valley. Three hulking shapes come crashing through the bathhouses — oni scouts, near twice a man's height, hide the color of bruised plums, iron-studded clubs in their fists and tusks jutting from leering mouths. They wade into the holy spring and begin to foul it, laughing, while pilgrims scatter screaming. One turns its yellow eyes on you and grins. 'More climbers,' it rumbles. 'The King will be pleased. None come down from the mountain now.'"

skillChecks.success: You roar a challenge that makes the oni focus on you, drawing them away from the fleeing pilgrims and the spring.
skillChecks.failure: The oni ignore your bluster and continue toward the pilgrims and the sacred water.

skillChecks.success: You use the slick, steaming terrain to your advantage, repositioning past an oni without provoking a swing.
skillChecks.failure: You slip on the wet stone and must spend movement to right yourself.

enemies: 3 oni scouts (use ogre stats, reflavored as oni)
1 oni brute-leader (use ogre with a club doing an extra 1d8, or a half-ogre, as the scout-captain)
combatEncounters.tactics: The oni are brutal and direct — they target the most lightly-armored characters and try to hurl them into the scalding spring (a shove contest; failure means 1d6 fire damage from the boiling water). The leader hangs back to coordinate, bellowing for the others to cut off the party's healers. They fight without fear but will retreat up the trail if reduced below a third of their number, fleeing to warn the upper stations.
combatEncounters.terrain: A maze of bathhouses, stone basins, and slick wet walkways wreathed in steam (lightly obscured, granting partial concealment). The scalding spring basins are a hazard: anyone shoved in takes 1d6 fire damage. Wooden bathhouse walls are flammable cover.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The party's first real taste of the Oni-King's host. Play the oni as cruel but not stupid — they use the terrain, target weak links, and try to defile the spring as a secondary objective (if the party ignores them, the onsen is poisoned and loses its restorative power for the rest of the adventure). Let an oni that flees carry word upslope, raising the stakes for Act 3. Award XP per the post-combat checklist.
loot: Oni iron-studded clubs (sellable as curios, 15 gp each)
A pilgrim's pouch the oni stole, holding 35 gp and a Potion of Healing
An iron tag stamped with the Oni-King's mark — a clue that names the demon lord Akki-no-Kami

scenes.name: The Cedar Ascent
scenes.description: The party climbs the pilgrim trail through ancient cedar forest, past the First through Fifth Stations, having their staves branded and gathering blessings. The lower slopes are gentle but the demons' presence grows: a station burns, tengu raiders harry the switchbacks, and at the Fifth Station the great trees thin away and the first thin, cold air bites.
scenes.readAloud: "The trail climbs in long switchbacks through cedar forest older than any kingdom, the trees so vast that three of you together could not span one trunk. At each station — small huts and weathered shrines — a keeper brands your walking-staff with the station's mark and bows you onward and upward. Pilgrim bells ring faintly through the green gloom. But the higher you climb, the wronger it feels: a shrine-fire snuffed out, a station hut standing empty, claw-marks raked across a trail-marker. And then, from the canopy above, you hear the harsh caw of crows that are too large and too clever to be crows at all — and the trees begin to thin, and ahead the green gives way to bare red gravel where the world above the forest begins."

skillChecks.success: You spot the tengu raiders gathering in the high cedar boughs before they strike, granting the party a surprise-free, prepared encounter.
skillChecks.failure: The tengu attack from above before the party is ready (they have surprise in the first round).

skillChecks.success: You pace the climb wisely, resting at each station and pressing the shrine-blessings in order — the party begins the upper slopes with one level of resistance to the demon-cold.
skillChecks.failure: You push too hard, too fast; the thin air at the Fifth Station leaves the party fatigued (disadvantage on the first Constitution save of Act 3).

skillChecks.success: When demon-loosened scree gives way in a small landslide, you scramble clear and haul a stumbling ally to safety.
skillChecks.failure: The landslide catches you; take 2d6 bludgeoning damage and slide 15 feet down the slope.

enemies: 5 tengu raiders (use harpy stats, reflavored as crow-winged mountain demons)
2 tengu adepts (use harpy with a short-range gust attack, or swap in 2 swarms of ravens for chaff)
combatEncounters.tactics: The tengu dive from the high cedars, using hit-and-run flight to harry the party along the narrow switchbacks. They try to knock characters off the trail edge (a shove toward a 20-foot drop: 2d6 falling damage and a climb back up) and to scatter the party rather than stand and fight. They cackle and mock in human voices. They break off and wheel away into the canopy if half are slain.
combatEncounters.terrain: Narrow switchback trail with a steep forested drop on the downhill side (20-30 ft falls). The cedar canopy gives the flying tengu cover and high ground. A burning station hut at the encounter's edge spreads fire each round and holds trapped pilgrims who can be rescued.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene compresses the lower-mountain climb into a single dramatic ascent with a flying skirmish and a moral choice (fight the tengu, or break off to rescue the pilgrims and keeper from the burning hut?). Reward parties who split focus to save lives. The Fifth Station is the threshold: describe the cedars giving way to bare volcanic gravel and the first noticeable shortness of breath, setting up the altitude hazards of Act 3. The hidden kakemono scroll (from the Lower Slopes location secrets) can be found with a keeper here.
loot: The kakemono scroll-painting of Fuji that reveals the demon-gate's location at the crater's eastern lip (key clue)
A station keeper's gift: 3 sets of straw crampons that grant advantage on saves against the cinder-slope's difficult terrain
Tengu feathers and a stolen jade comb worth 30 gp recovered from the raiders

acts.title: Act 3: The Killing Cold and the Ash Stations ❄️🏔️
acts.description: Above the treeline, Fuji turns lethal. The party climbs the upper stations through thin air, freezing wind, and the Oni-King's entrenched shock-troops, enduring altitude and exposure hazards as they fight toward the summit. This act is a grueling, attritional climb with two hard combats and persistent environmental danger — honest hazards that can wound or kill if ignored.
objectives: Endure the altitude-sickness and cold-exposure hazards of the upper slopes
Break the oni shock-troops holding the Eighth Station
Survive or evade the yuki-onna luring climbers to freeze
Reach the Ninth Station and prepare for the pre-dawn summit push

scenes.name: The Cinder Slope and the Thin Air
scenes.description: Above the Fifth Station, the cedars vanish and Fuji becomes a near-vertical slope of red-black volcanic cinder, raked by freezing wind. The air grows thin enough to steal the breath, and the cold bites with a malice that is more than natural. The party must manage the climb's escalating hazards — altitude sickness and frostbite — station by station.
scenes.readAloud: "There are no more trees. The world has become a single endless slope of red-black cinder rising into a sky gone hard and pale, and the wind comes down off the summit like a blade, carrying the reek of sulphur and something colder underneath — a cold that does not belong to any winter. Each step sinks ankle-deep in loose gravel; each breath comes shorter and thinner than the last, and your head begins to pound with the altitude. Far above, the stone huts of the upper stations cling to the slope like barnacles, their lamps the only warmth in all that desolation. And the cold keeps deepening, unnaturally, as if the mountain itself is being drained of its fire."

skillChecks.success: You acclimatize to the thin air at this station and climb on without ill effect. (Repeat at the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Stations; the DC rises by 1 each station.)
skillChecks.failure: Altitude sickness sets in: you gain one level of exhaustion. Resting a full hour at a station's lamp removes it.

skillChecks.success: You shrug off the unnatural demon-cold (advantage if you earned the trail-shrine blessings or carry a charcoal hand-warmer).
skillChecks.failure: Frostbite: take 1d6 cold damage and have disadvantage on Dexterity checks until you warm up at a station.

skillChecks.success: You find the safest line up the shifting cinder and the sheltered lee of the wind, halving the party's exposure rolls for the next stretch.
skillChecks.failure: You lead the party across an exposed face; everyone rolls the cold-exposure save with disadvantage on this stretch.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene is the environment as antagonist. Make the altitude and cold real and mechanical, but FAIR — telegraph them at Hakone and the Fifth Station, and always provide outs: the station lamps, hand-warmers, the onsen-rest benefit, the trail-shrine blessings, the warrior-monk's grave at the Ninth Station. Exhaustion should bite but be recoverable with rest at the stations. Do NOT let the hazards become an unwinnable death-spiral; they are a resource-drain that raises tension before the boss, not a trap. If the party is suffering badly, the sheltered ice-cave behind the Eighth Station (a location secret) offers a safe long rest.
loot: The warrior-monk's grave at the Ninth Station yields a +1 naginata (glaive) blessed against oni, glowing faintly silver near demons
A frozen pilgrim's pack with 20 gp, a Potion of Greater Healing, and a fur-lined cloak (advantage vs. natural cold)

scenes.name: The Eighth Station — Demon Stronghold
scenes.description: The Oni-King has turned the Eighth Station into a forward war-camp. To climb higher, the party must break the oni shock-troops and their champion who hold the only sheltered hut on the upper slope — a brutal fight made worse by the thin air and cold.
scenes.readAloud: "The Eighth Station is a charnel-camp. The stone hut's roof has been torn off and a bonfire of broken shrine-timbers roars within, throwing demon-shadows huge against the cinder slope. Oni hunch around it gnawing on things you choose not to look at, and at their center stands one greater than the rest — a war-oni a full head taller, its skin the red of fresh blood, a great iron-banded kanabō club resting across one shoulder, a necklace of frozen pilgrim-charms at its throat. It rises as you approach, and its grin splits its face from tusk to tusk. 'You climbed farther than the others,' it says, almost admiring. 'Good. The higher you fall, the better you break.'"

skillChecks.success: Using the bonfire's glare and the howling wind, you slip into flanking positions, granting the party surprise and advantage on the first round.
skillChecks.failure: The wind shifts and an oni sentry spots you; no surprise, and the camp is roused.

skillChecks.success: You fight smart in the thin air, pacing your exertion; the party ignores the altitude's disadvantage for the duration of this combat.
skillChecks.failure: The exertion of battle at altitude tells: each character makes a DC 13 Constitution save at the end of the fight or gains a level of exhaustion.

enemies: 1 oni war-champion (use a true Oni stat block, MM, CR 7, OR an ogre with maximized HP and a 2d8 club for lower-level parties)
2 fire-imps (use imp stats, reflavored as ember-demons from the gate)
combatEncounters.tactics: The war-champion is a disciplined killer: it uses the bonfire's reach to herd the party, targets spellcasters, and uses its kanabō to knock characters prone before its lessers swarm them. The shock-troops try to hurl heroes off the camp's exposed downhill edge (a 40-foot fall to a ledge below: 4d6 bludgeoning). The fire-imps flit in to spit embers and turn invisible to reposition. The champion fights to the death — its honor will not let it flee from worthy foes. This is a genuinely dangerous fight; the dice are the dice. If the party is overmatched, retreat down to a lower station's lamp is always an option.
combatEncounters.terrain: A roofless stone hut on a narrow ledge, lit by a roaring bonfire (bright light in 20 ft; anyone shoved into it takes 2d6 fire). The downhill edge is a sheer 40-foot drop. Loose cinder underfoot is difficult terrain. Howling wind imposes disadvantage on ranged attacks beyond 30 feet.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The toughest fight before the boss — a true test of the party's resources and tactics at full peril. Honor the dice: if a character drops, run death saves straight. The war-champion is a worthy, almost honorable foe; it salutes a good hit and dies without complaint. Clearing the station opens the sheltered ice-cave behind it for a desperately-needed long rest before the summit push. Run the full post-combat checklist: XP for the Oni champion and its host, loot the bodies, update files immediately.
loot: The war-champion's kanabō: a greatclub that deals an extra 1d6 thunder on a hit (uncommon, attunement)
A necklace of frozen pilgrim-charms (worth 60 gp; returning it to the Hakone shrine later earns a blessing)
120 gp in looted coin and offerings, plus a jade demon-mask worth 75 gp
A war-map scratched on hide showing the demon-gate's position and the Oni-King's guard at the crater rim

scenes.name: The Snow-Woman's Lullaby
scenes.description: On the bitter climb between the Eighth and Ninth Stations, a yuki-onna — a snow-woman of heartbreaking beauty — drifts out of the blizzard, her voice a lullaby that beckons the weary to lie down in the warm-seeming snow and never rise. The party must resist her call, save any who succumb, and decide whether to fight or flee her.
scenes.readAloud: "The wind drops, and into the sudden stillness comes a voice — a woman's voice, low and sweet, singing a lullaby that wraps around your aching limbs like a warm quilt. She drifts out of the snow toward you: a woman of impossible beauty, white as the drifts, her kimono trailing frost, her bare feet leaving no print. Her smile is kind. Her eyes are black and bottomless. 'You are so tired,' she murmurs, and oh, it is true. 'Lie down. Rest a while in the snow. I will keep you warm.' And the warm-seeming snow at your feet suddenly looks like the softest bed you have ever seen."

skillChecks.success: You recognize the lullaby for the death-charm it is and tear your mind free of it.
skillChecks.failure: You are charmed: you begin walking toward the snow-woman to lie down in the snow (which deals 1d6 cold at the start of each of your turns). Allies can shake you free with an action and a DC 13 check, or by damaging you.

skillChecks.success: You see the grief beneath her cruelty — she was once a pilgrim who froze on this slope, and a kind word or a shared warmth (a charcoal hand-warmer offered freely) may turn her aside without a fight.
skillChecks.failure: She seems only a monster of the cold.

enemies: 1 yuki-onna (use will-o'-wisp stats for the luring/charm phase, escalating to a reflavored ice mephit swarm or a single CR 5 cold-elemental if combat is forced)
combatEncounters.tactics: The yuki-onna prefers seduction to slaughter: she charms one character at a time and walks them toward the killing snow, staying at range and turning translucent (incorporeal) to avoid blows. If the party shows her genuine compassion (the Insight route — a freely-given warmth, a promise to carry word of her name down the mountain), she weeps, releases all charmed characters, and fades, leaving a parting gift. If attacked without mercy, she fights with chilling fury but can be destroyed.
combatEncounters.terrain: A whiteout blizzard on an open slope (heavily obscured beyond 30 ft; ranged attacks at disadvantage). Deep, warm-seeming snowdrifts that deal 1d6 cold per round to anyone lying in them. No natural shelter — the Ninth Station's lamp glows faintly ahead as a goal.

scenes.roleplayNotes: A haunting encounter offering a compassion-route in the tradition of the campaign's themes. The yuki-onna is tragic, not merely monstrous — a frozen pilgrim's sorrow given form. Reward players who see her grief and answer it with kindness (the Insight + a freely given hand-warmer or warm word ends the encounter peacefully and earns her blessing). But honor player agency: if they choose to fight, run it honestly. Either way, surviving her brings the party to the Ninth Station and the threshold of the summit.
loot: If shown compassion: the yuki-onna's frost-tear, a gem that, shattered, ends one creature's burning or grants the party resistance to fire for 1 minute (single use — invaluable at the fiery summit)
A frozen traveler's cache she guarded: 40 gp and a scroll of Protection from Energy

acts.title: Act 4: The Summit Crater and the Breaking of the Crown 🌋👹💀
acts.description: Before dawn, the party crests Fuji's summit crater to face the Oni-King Akki-no-Kami at his demon-gate. This is the campaign's climactic battle: an epic boss fight against a demon-lord and his honor-guard, fought on a steaming crater rim against a rising tide of lesser demons, with the holy sunrise — goraikō — and the dragon's tide-blessing offering the means to seal the gate and end the war. Honest dice; a TPK is a valid, un-rigged outcome. Glory or death at the roof of the world.
objectives: Crest the summit crater in the pre-dawn dark
Hold against the Oni-King's honor-guard and the demons pouring from the gate
Break the Oni-King's iron crown to weaken his hold on the gate
Channel the dragon's tide-blessing through goraikō at the moment of dawn to seal the demon-gate
Decide the fate of the mountain and the Floating World

scenes.name: The Crater Rim Before Dawn
scenes.description: In the freezing dark before sunrise, the party hauls itself over the crater's lip and beholds the full horror of the Oni-King's work: a molten demon-gate torn into the crater's eastern wall, lesser demons swarming from it, and Akki-no-Kami himself enthroned on the rim, waiting. The holy sunrise — goraikō — is less than an hour away.
scenes.readAloud: "You crest the final ridge in the killing cold of the hour before dawn, and the summit opens before you — a vast crater of cracked black stone wreathed in sulphurous steam, ringed with the toppled shrines of a thousand years of pilgrims. And it has been profaned. At the crater's eastern lip, a wound has been torn into the world itself: a fissure of molten red light, roaring like a furnace, and through it pour demons — small and burning, crawling and capering, a tide of them spreading across the rim. And there, upon a throne of shattered shrine-stone above the gate, sits their king. Akki-no-Kami. The Oni-King. Vast as an oak, his skin the black-red of cooling lava, two great horns sweeping back from a brow crowned with a band of black iron that drinks the firelight. He sees you. And he begins, slowly, to laugh. 'Pilgrims,' he says, and the word shakes the stones. 'You climbed all this way... to watch the world burn. How devout.' To the east, the black sky has just begun, faintly, to pale."

skillChecks.success: You read the demon-gate's structure and understand the seal: the Oni-King's iron crown anchors it, and the gate can only be closed by overwhelming holy light — such as goraikō channeled through the dragon's tide-blessing — at the exact moment of dawn.
skillChecks.failure: The gate is clearly the source of the demons, but how to close it eludes you until the dawn nears.

skillChecks.success: You feel the mountain-god's smothered presence beneath the crater and the approach of goraikō; you know the holy sunrise is the key, and roughly how long until it breaks (telegraphing the dawn-clock for the players).
skillChecks.failure: You sense holiness fighting through the corruption but cannot time it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Set the stage with maximum grandeur. Make the dawn-clock explicit and mechanical: goraikō will break in roughly 6-8 rounds of combat. The party must SURVIVE to dawn and then use the tide-blessing to seal the gate at the moment the sun crests the eastern rim. Make clear (via the Arcana/Religion checks, or Jirō's earlier words, or Ryūjin's instructions) that they are NOT required to kill the Oni-King to win — sealing the gate at dawn ends the demon tide and breaks his power — but he will fight to stop them, so a confrontation is unavoidable. This framing lets the boss fight be epic without being a slog: the win condition is the seal, not a hit-point race to zero, though killing the King is also a valid path. Let the players choose their plan before initiative.

scenes.name: The Battle for the Crater — The Oni-King Akki-no-Kami
scenes.description: The climactic battle. The party fights Akki-no-Kami and his demon honor-guard on the steaming crater rim while lesser demons pour from the gate each round and the dawn-clock ticks toward goraikō. Breaking the King's iron crown slows the demon tide; surviving to dawn and channeling the tide-blessing seals the gate.
scenes.readAloud: "The Oni-King rises from his throne, and the iron crown on his brow flares with stolen fire. 'Come then, little pilgrims,' Akki-no-Kami roars, hefting a kanabō the size of a fallen pine. 'Let us see what you are worth — here, at the roof of the world, where heaven and the furnace meet!' Behind him the gate howls and vomits forth fresh demons, and far to the east, the first thin blade of gold cuts the horizon. The dawn is coming. The question is whether any of you will live to see it. 💀"

skillChecks.success: You make a daring leap or shove that uses the crater's steam-vents and ledges against a demon, hurling it into the fissure (instantly destroying a lesser demon, or dealing 3d6 fire to a larger one).
skillChecks.failure: Your gambit fails and you must make a DC 14 Dexterity save or take 1d6 fire from a venting jet yourself.

skillChecks.skill: Attack Roll (Called Shot at the Crown)
skillChecks.success: On a deliberate strike at the Oni-King's head (attack at disadvantage, OR any natural 20 against him), you knock the iron crown from his brow: the demon-gate's output halves, fewer demons spawn each round, and the Oni-King is enraged but weakened (his AC drops by 2).
skillChecks.failure: Your strike rings off the crown without dislodging it.

skillChecks.success: At the precise moment goraikō breaks over the eastern rim, you raise the dragon's tide-blessing and channel the holy sunrise through it into the gate; the fissure shrieks and slams shut, severing the Oni-King from his power. This is the victory condition.
skillChecks.failure: Your timing is off by a heartbeat; the gate flickers but holds. You may try again the next round, but the demon tide surges once more in the meantime.

enemies: 1 Oni-King Akki-no-Kami (BOSS — use a buffed Oni / Fire Giant hybrid, CR 9-10: high HP, multiattack with a kanabō for 2d8+5 bludgeoning, a recharge fire-breath cone for 6d6, Innate Spellcasting for darkness/charm; legendary-style: he may take one extra attack at the end of a random character's turn while crowned)
2 oni honor-guard (true Oni stats, CR 7, or ogre-champions for lower-level parties)
Lesser demons from the gate: 1d4 fire-imps spawn at the start of each round until the crown is broken (then halve the rate), and until the gate is sealed
combatEncounters.tactics: Akki-no-Kami is a furnace given form and pride given a crown. He opens with his fire-breath cone, then wades into melee against whoever struck him hardest, using darkness to blind ranged attackers and his Change Shape (Oni trait) to feign a wounded retreat and ambush a straggler. He prizes single combat and will honor a challenge, peeling off from the group to duel a worthy champion — use this to give the party tactical openings. His iron crown is his anchor to the gate: a called shot (disadvantage) or any natural 20 against him can knock it loose, halving the demon spawn-rate and dropping his AC by 2. He grows reckless and wrathful as dawn nears, sensing his power slipping. HONEST DICE: he does not cheat, and neither do the players — if the party falls, run death saves and let a TPK stand as a valid, un-rigged ending. But the win condition is mercy on the action-economy: SEALING THE GATE AT DAWN ends the demon tide and breaks the King's power even if he still lives, so the party need not grind his full HP to zero to win. Track the dawn-clock openly (6-8 rounds to goraikō); build the tension round by round.
combatEncounters.terrain: A steaming crater rim of cracked obsidian ringed with toppled shrines (cover). Steam-vents jet randomly: at the start of each round, one 10-ft area chosen by the DM erupts, dealing 1d6 fire to anyone in it (DC 13 Dex save for half) — usable against enemies via shove. The molten demon-gate at the eastern lip deals 3d6 fire to anyone shoved into it (and destroys lesser demons so flung). The eastern rim is where goraikō breaks: a character must reach it and have line to the rising sun to channel the tide-blessing seal.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THE FINALE. Make it cinematic, make it brutal, make it FAIR. Run the dawn-clock out loud so the players feel the seconds. Reward the three pillars of the fight: (1) controlling the demon tide by breaking the crown, (2) surviving the King's onslaught, and (3) timing the seal to goraikō. Honor every die — natural 20s are critical hits and dramatic crown-strikes; natural 1s are honest fumbles. Do NOT fabricate HP, do NOT invent a deus ex machina, and do NOT rig the King to be unkillable OR to whiff on purpose. If the party is winning, let them win gloriously; if they are losing, let them retreat down the mountain (a valid choice) or fall with honor (a valid TPK). The dragon's tide-blessing and goraikō are the intended path to a clean victory without a 200-HP grind — but they are tools the players must USE, not guarantees. After the gate seals at dawn, the demons remaining collapse to ash and the surviving Oni-King (if any) is mortal and beatable, or flees broken. Run the full post-encounter and session-end checklists.
loot: Akki-no-Kami's iron crown — once cleansed at a shrine, a Circlet of demon-warding (advantage on saves vs. fiends; attunement)
His kanabō — Demonbane, a +1 greatclub that deals an extra 2d6 radiant to fiends
A hoard of pilgrim-offerings the King had defiled: 600 gp in coin, gems, and lacquerware
The mountain-god's freed blessing: each surviving hero gains the Mountain's Favor (one auto-success on a death save, once, before the campaign ends)

scenes.name: Goraikō — The Holy Sunrise
scenes.description: With the demon-gate sealed and the Oni-King broken, the holy sunrise breaks fully over the crater rim. The mountain-god stirs awake, the demons are gone to ash, and the party stands at the roof of the world in the first clean light. The denouement: the fate of the mountain, the Floating World, and the heroes themselves.
scenes.readAloud: "The gate slams shut with a sound like the world's last door closing, and silence rushes in. The demon-fires gutter and die; the steam thins; the killing cold breaks like a fever. And then — the sun. Goraikō. The holy sunrise crests the eastern rim in a flood of pure gold, pouring across the crater, across the sea of clouds spread out far below you, across your battered, breathing, living faces. Beneath your feet you feel something vast and gentle stir — the mountain-god, waking, freed. A warmth rises through the stone like a long-held breath finally released. You have climbed to the roof of the Floating World, and you have not let it burn. The deer of Itsukushima will graze in peace. The torii will float upon the tide. And the dawn — the dawn is so very beautiful. Kirei, the pilgrims would say. Kirei. ⛩️🌅"

skillChecks.success: You offer thanks to the waking mountain-god in the proper form; the god's favor settles over the party as a lasting blessing (the DM may grant each hero a one-time boon of their choosing in the campaign's epilogue).
skillChecks.failure: You stand in awed silence, which is honor enough; no mechanical boon, but the moment is no less sacred.

skillChecks.success: In the clean light you understand what the climb cost and what it bought — and you carry that wisdom down the mountain, a changed person.
skillChecks.failure: The enormity of it has not yet sunk in; it will, in time.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The denouement and emotional release after the climactic battle. Let the players breathe, mourn any fallen, and take in goraikō from the summit. Tie off the threads: Ryūjin-no-Musume's tide-blessing spent to save the world; Jirō the guide vindicated; the yuki-onna's grief (if she was shown mercy) eased by the mountain-god's waking; the Hakone springs and Itsukushima's torii safe once more. Award the final milestone XP for the campaign's climax. Then provide the session-end / campaign-end save summary. If a TPK occurred, narrate it with gravity and respect — the heroes who fell on Fuji's summit holding back the demon-tide are remembered forever in the shrines below, and the player may reset characters to begin anew. The dice are the dice. 💀⛩️
loot: The Mountain-God's Blessing: a lasting boon for each surviving hero (DM's discretion — a permanent +1 to one saving throw, or one casting of a 3rd-level spell per long rest, or similar campaign-capstone reward)
A pilgrim's summit-brand burned into each surviving hero's staff, marking them forever as those who climbed Fuji and saved the Floating World

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima island (near Hiroshima) has a giant vermilion torii gate built out over tidal flats. At HIGH tide it appears to float on the sea; at LOW tide the water recedes and you can walk out across the wet sand right up to the gate and touch its base. The shrine and its walkways are likewise built on stilts over the water. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Japan's classic 'three views.' Check a tide table before you visit so you can see both the floating high-tide view and the walk-up low-tide view.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: There is no sea-dragon's daughter (Ryūjin-no-Musume) guarding it, no tide-gate that ferries pilgrims to Mt. Fuji in a night, and no drowned-dead (umibōzu) rising from the flats. Ryūjin the dragon-god of the sea is from real Japanese mythology, but he does not, in reality, grant blessings to adventurers.

culturalCodex.topic: Miyajima's wild deer and momiji-manjū cakes
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Miyajima island is home to friendly, semi-tame wild deer that wander freely among visitors (don't feed them — and watch your maps and tickets, they'll nibble paper!). The island's famous local sweet is momiji-manjū: small maple-leaf-shaped cakes filled with red bean paste, custard, chocolate, and other fillings, often sold freshly grilled. 'Momiji' means maple/autumn leaves.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the adventure, eating a maple-leaf cake restores a hit point and morale — in reality it just tastes great. The deer are not magically tame guardians, just habituated wildlife (give them space and respect).

culturalCodex.topic: Climbing Mt. Fuji — the official season ONLY
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Mt. Fuji (Fuji-san, 3,776 m) can be safely climbed by ordinary hikers ONLY during the official season, roughly early July to early September, when the mountain huts and trails are open and staffed. Outside that window the upper mountain is snow-covered, brutally cold, and genuinely deadly — it kills unprepared climbers most years. Recent rules also include trail fees and reservation/crowd-control systems on the popular Yoshida route. Always check the current official season dates and regulations before planning.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: No Oni-King (Akki-no-Kami) has seized the summit, there is no demon-gate at the crater, and you cannot seal anything with a magic pearl at dawn. The mountain-god is a real object of reverence; the demon warlord is invented for the story.

culturalCodex.topic: The numbered stations and mountain huts
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: The Mt. Fuji trails are divided into ten numbered 'stations' (gōme). Most climbers start at the Fifth Station (around 2,300-2,400 m, reachable by road/bus) rather than the base, and climb past numbered huts (mountain lodges) where you can rest, buy water and food at high prices, use toilets, and even sleep overnight. Booking a hut in advance is strongly recommended in season. Staffs ('kongō-zue') can be branded with each station's mark as a souvenir of your climb.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The stations in the adventure are besieged by tengu and oni and one hides a warrior-monk's blessed naginata. In reality they're staffed lodges selling noodles and selling you a warm bunk — no demons, just other tired hikers.

culturalCodex.topic: Altitude sickness on Fuji is real
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Altitude sickness (headache, nausea, dizziness, shortness of breath) is a genuine and common risk on Mt. Fuji because of the rapid ascent to nearly 3,800 m. The standard advice is to ascend slowly, spend time acclimatizing at the Fifth Station before climbing, stay hydrated, and consider an overnight at a hut rather than a non-stop 'bullet climb.' Descend if symptoms get bad. Portable oxygen cans are sold but aren't a real fix — pacing and acclimatization are.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the game, altitude is modeled as Constitution saves and exhaustion levels, and the cold is partly 'demon-cold.' In reality the cold and thin air are entirely natural — and a charcoal hand-warmer ('kairo') really does help with the cold, even if it won't ward off a snow-woman.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: 'Goraikō' (御来光) is the revered sunrise seen from near or atop Mt. Fuji, often above a sea of clouds. Many climbers time their ascent to reach the summit in the pre-dawn hours specifically to witness it — it's a genuine highlight and a spiritual experience for pilgrims. Dress for serious cold and wind at the top even in summer; it can be near freezing at the summit while warm at the base.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: Goraikō cannot be 'channeled' through a dragon's pearl to seal a demon-gate. The holy-light-seals-the-portal mechanic is pure fantasy; the sunrise's beauty and spiritual weight, however, are completely real.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Hakone, in the foothills southeast of Mt. Fuji, is a famous hot-spring (onsen) resort town with views of Fuji on clear days, a lake (Ashinoko) with sightseeing boats, ropeways over volcanic vents (Owakudani), and many ryokan inns with mineral baths. It's a popular relaxing stop on the way to or from the Fuji area. Onsen etiquette: wash thoroughly before entering the communal bath, no swimsuits, and note that many baths have rules about tattoos.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: Hakone's onsen do not remove a level of exhaustion in game-mechanical terms, oni do not raid the baths, and the waters don't glow when a mountain stirs. The soothing, restorative feeling of a real onsen soak, though — that part the game gets right in spirit.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: 'yama' (山) = mountain (as in Fuji-yama / Fuji-san). 'umi' (海) = sea. 'kirei' (綺麗) = beautiful/clean/pretty — a great word to exclaim at a view or a sunrise. 'tasukete!' (助けて) = help! (a genuine emergency cry). Other handy ones: 'arigatō' = thank you, 'sumimasen' = excuse me/sorry, 'kanpai' = cheers, 'oishii' = delicious. Politeness and a small bow go a long way.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the adventure these words flavor the narration ('kirei' at goraikō, 'tasukete!' from imperiled pilgrims). They're real, useful phrases — but learning them won't summon a sea-dragon or ward off a yuki-onna, sadly.

npcsInvolved.name: Ryūjin-no-Musume (The Sea-Dragon's Daughter)
npcsInvolved.description: First met as a young miko in white and crimson at the Itsukushima shrine, she is in truth the daughter of Ryūjin, the dragon-god who holds the sea. In her true form she is vast and serpentine, scaled in pearl and storm-grey, with eyes like deep green tide-pools. She is ancient, grave, and unexpectedly gentle, valuing honesty and compassion over strength or flattery.
npcsInvolved.motivation: She guards the tide-gate of the floating torii and judges who is worthy to receive its blessing. With the mountain-god silenced and the Floating World threatened, she seeks champions who climb to protect others rather than for glory. She will spend her precious tide-blessing only on those who prove their hearts true — and she keeps her promises absolutely, including a vow of one rescue at sea.

npcsInvolved.name: Jirō the Mountain Guide
npcsInvolved.description: A weathered old man tending a teahouse at the foot of the climb in Hakone, his face mapped with the wind and sun of a lifetime on the mountain. He climbed Fuji as a young man and glimpsed the demon-gate at the crater — a sight he has never spoken of until now. He is gruff, wary of outsiders, but deeply kind beneath it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Jirō wants the mountain and its pilgrims protected, and he carries a quiet guilt for never warning anyone of what he saw at the summit decades ago. He shares his hard-won knowledge of the stations, the altitude, and the demon-gate with those who earn his trust, and gives away his treasured fear-warding charm to whoever seems steadiest for the climb.

npcsInvolved.name: The Yuki-onna (Snow-Woman)
npcsInvolved.description: A woman of impossible, frost-pale beauty who drifts out of the upper-mountain blizzards, her kimono trailing rime, her bare feet leaving no print, her eyes black and bottomless. Her voice is a lullaby that beckons the weary to lie down in the snow forever. She was once a pilgrim who froze to death on the slope, her sorrow given form by the demon-cold.
npcsInvolved.motivation: She lures the exhausted to a warm-seeming death in the snow, repeating the fate that claimed her. But beneath the cruelty is grief, not malice. Shown genuine compassion — a freely-given warmth, a promise to carry her name down the mountain — she releases her victims, weeps, and fades, leaving a parting gift. Attacked without mercy, she fights with chilling fury.

npcsInvolved.name: Akki-no-Kami, the Oni-King
npcsInvolved.description: A demon-lord vast as an ancient oak, his skin the black-red of cooling lava, two great horns sweeping back from a brow crowned with a band of black iron that anchors his demon-gate. He wields a kanabō the size of a fallen pine and laughs with a voice that shakes the summit stones. He is proud, cruel, and — in his own monstrous way — honorable, prizing single combat against worthy foes.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Akki-no-Kami has seized the silenced mountain-god's crater and torn open a demon-gate, intending to crack the seal of the fire-mountain and drown the Floating World below in ash and flame. His iron crown binds him to the gate and to his power; break the crown, seal the gate at dawn, and his reign over the summit ends. He fights to the death against any he deems worthy, and will not flee an honorable challenge while crowned.

rewards.gold: Roughly 1,650 gp total across the adventure (sea-pearls, looted oni hoards, the King's defiled pilgrim-offerings of 600 gp, and assorted gems and lacquerware)
items: The Tide-Blessing (plot key — seals the demon-gate at goraikō)
Akki-no-Kami's iron crown, cleansed into a Circlet of demon-warding (attunement)
Demonbane — the Oni-King's +1 greatclub dealing +2d6 radiant to fiends
The yuki-onna's frost-tear (fire-resistance, single use) if she was shown mercy
The Mountain-God's Blessing (campaign-capstone boon for each surviving hero)
Assorted Potions of Healing/Greater Healing, holy water, and a scroll of Protection from Energy
rewards.story: The heroes have climbed to the roof of the Floating World and held back the demon-tide at the very edge of dawn. By passing the sea-dragon's trial, enduring Fuji's killing cold, and sealing the Oni-King's gate as goraikō broke, they have freed the mountain-god, saved Itsukushima's floating torii and Hakone's springs, and earned places in the shrines' memory forever. The fate of any compassion shown (to the yuki-onna, to fallen foes) and any mercy or vengeance dealt to the broken Oni-King will color the epilogue of the Floating World — and the summit-brand on each hero's staff marks them as legends for whatever adventures may follow.

twists: The gentle young miko who greets the party at Itsukushima is no servant but Ryūjin-no-Musume herself, the sea-dragon's daughter, wearing a mortal shape to judge the worthiness of pilgrims.

Victory at the summit does NOT require grinding the Oni-King's hit points to zero — sealing the demon-gate at the exact moment of goraikō (the holy sunrise), using the dragon's tide-blessing, severs his power and ends the demon tide even if he still lives. The win condition is timing and mercy on the action-economy, not a pure damage race.

The Oni-King's iron crown, not his body, is the true anchor of his power; a called shot or a critical hit that knocks it from his brow halves the demon tide and weakens him — rewarding clever tactics over brute force.

The yuki-onna who kills weary climbers is not a monster but a frozen pilgrim's grief given form; she can be laid to rest with compassion rather than steel, and her gift may prove vital at the fiery summit.

Several encounters (the drowned-dead at the torii, the yuki-onna, the Oni-King himself) offer a non-combat or partial-combat resolution to players who respect the rites, read the tides, and answer cruelty with kindness — the Floating World rewards reverence.
dmTips: Run the tide as a living clock in Act 1 and the dawn (goraikō) as a living clock in Act 4. Announce the count out loud — 'two rounds until the flats flood,' 'the sun is four rounds from cresting the rim' — so the players feel the pressure and can plan around it. The clocks, not the monsters, are the real tension.

Telegraph the altitude and cold hazards early (at Hakone and the Fifth Station) so they never feel like a gotcha, and ALWAYS provide outs: station lamps, charcoal hand-warmers, the onsen-rest benefit, the trail-shrine blessings, the ice-cave long rest. Exhaustion should bite but stay recoverable. Do not let the hazards become an unwinnable death-spiral — they are a resource drain that raises tension before the boss, not a trap.

HONOR THE DICE at the summit. The boss fight is designed to be epic and dangerous, not rigged. Do not fabricate hit points to keep the Oni-King alive, do not invent a last-second rescue, and do not have him whiff on purpose. If the party falls, run death saves straight and let a TPK stand as a valid, respectful ending — the heroes who fell holding the rim are remembered in the shrines below, and the player can reset and begin anew. The dawn-seal and tide-blessing exist so a smart party can win cleanly without a 200-HP grind — but they are tools the players must USE, not guarantees.

Scale the boss to the party's actual level and size. For a level-7 party, use a single buffed Oni (CR 7) plus chaff; for level 9-10, use the Oni/Fire Giant hybrid described, or two Oni and a Fire Giant. Adjust the lesser-demon spawn rate from the gate to keep the action economy tense but survivable. The goal is a fight that feels deadly and is honestly winnable — never a foregone conclusion in either direction.

Lean into the two-stage structure: Act 1 (Itsukushima) is wonder, ritual, and a tide-puzzle; Acts 2-4 (Fuji) are an attritional climb building to the boss. Use the culturalCodex to flavor the narration with real, evocative detail (the floating torii, the tame deer, goraikō, the station huts) while keeping the fantasy elements clearly the stuff of story. Sprinkle the real Japanese phrases ('kirei' at the sunrise, 'tasukete!' from imperiled pilgrims) for texture.

Offer the compassion-routes (the respectful offering at the torii, mercy for the yuki-onna, honoring a fallen foe) but never force them. Players who answer the Floating World's reverence in kind should be rewarded with blessings and easier paths; players who choose steel should find honest, winnable fights. Both are valid ways through the story.
